exercises.name: intro1
exercises.description:
This exercise introduces a simple Hello World module in Move for the Sui blockchain.
Your task is to ensure the module compiles successfully.

exercises.name: variables1
exercises.description:
This exercise requires the module to compile successfully.
Fix the syntax error in the function.

exercises.name: module1
exercises.description:
==== MODULE DECLARATION EXERCISE ====
A Move module must be declared with `module <address>::<name> { … }`.
In Move, functions are private by default. To call them from other modules,
they must be marked as `public`.

Your task:
Make the `greet` function public so the test module can call it.
(Hint: Add the `public` keyword before `fun`)

When the file compiles **and** the test passes you are done.

exercises.name: module2
exercises.description:
==== MODULE IMPORT EXERCISE ====
Move lets you `use` a function from another module.
The runner-crate contains a tiny helper module that we can import.

Your task:
1. Add a `use` statement to import `math::add`.
2. Implement `sum_three` using the imported `add` function.

The helper module is automatically available because the
runner-crate’s Move.toml publishes it at address `suilings`.

exercises.name: module3
exercises.hint:
Import vector with: use std::vector;
Then use vector::empty(), vector::push_back()
exercises.description:
==== MODULE IMPORTS EXERCISE ====
In Move, you can use functions and types from other modules by importing them.
The `use` statement allows you to bring items into scope.

Your task:
1. Import the `vector` module from the standard library
2. Use it to create and return a vector with the numbers 1, 2, 3

exercises.name: primitives1
exercises.hint:
u8 holds 0-255, u64 holds much larger numbers.
For add_numbers, use: a + b
exercises.description:
==== PRIMITIVE TYPES EXERCISE ====
Move has several integer types: u8, u16, u32, u64, u128, u256
Each type has a specific range of values it can hold.

Your task:
Fix the type annotations to make the code compile.

exercises.name: primitives2
exercises.hint:
Use comparison operators: >=, <=, &&
Example: age >= 18 && is_citizen
exercises.description:
==== BOOLEAN OPERATIONS EXERCISE ====
Booleans in Move are represented by the `bool` type.
Common operations: && (and), || (or), ! (not), == (equal), != (not equal)

Your task:
Implement the boolean logic functions below.

exercises.name: structs1
exercises.description:
==== STRUCTS EXERCISE ====
Structs allow you to create custom data types with named fields.
Syntax: struct Name { field1: Type1, field2: Type2 }

Your task:
1. Complete the Person struct with age and name fields
2. Implement the create_person function to instantiate the struct

exercises.name: structs2
exercises.hint:
Abilities are added after struct name: struct Name has copy, drop { ... }
- drop: can be destroyed
- copy: can be copied
- store: can be stored in other structs
exercises.description:
==== STRUCT ABILITIES EXERCISE ====
Structs in Move can have abilities: copy, drop, store, and key
- copy: The value can be copied
- drop: The value can be dropped/destroyed
- store: The value can be stored inside other structs
- key: The value can be used as a key for global storage

Your task:
Add the correct abilities to each struct based on the requirements

exercises.name: structs3
exercises.description:
==== NESTED STRUCTS EXERCISE ====
Structs can contain other structs as fields.
This allows you to build complex data structures.

Your task:
Complete the nested struct definitions and implement the functions

exercises.name: structs4
exercises.hint:
Use & for read-only: account.balance
Use &mut for modification: account.balance = new_value
Access fields through reference: account.field_name
exercises.description:
==== STRUCT METHODS & BORROWING EXERCISE ====
In Move, you can pass structs by reference (&) or mutable reference (&mut).
- & allows reading but not modifying
- &mut allows both reading and modifying

Your task:
Implement functions that work with struct references

exercises.name: structs5
exercises.description:
==== GENERIC STRUCTS EXERCISE ====
Generics allow you to write structs that work with any type.
Syntax: struct Name<T> { field: T }
You can also constrain generics with abilities: <T: copy + drop>

Your task:
Complete the generic struct definitions and implement the functions

exercises.name: functions1
exercises.hint:
multiply: return a * b
square: return num * num
max: use if (a > b) a else b
exercises.description:
==== FUNCTIONS EXERCISE ====
Functions in Move are declared with the `fun` keyword.
They can have parameters and return values.

Your task:
Implement the functions below following their specifications.

exercises.name: functions2
functions3
exercises.description:
==== MUTABLE REFERENCES EXERCISE ====
Functions can take mutable references (&mut) to modify values in place.
This is more efficient than copying large values.

Your task:
Implement functions that use mutable references

exercises.name: functions4
exercises.hint:
Generic function: fun name<T: drop>(value: T): T
Type constraints: <T: copy + drop>
Identity: just return value unchanged
exercises.description:
==== GENERIC FUNCTIONS EXERCISE ====
Generic functions work with any type that satisfies the specified constraints.
Syntax: fun name<T: ability>(param: T): T { ... }

Your task:
Implement generic functions that work with multiple types

exercises.name: functions5
exercises.description:
==== ADVANCED FUNCTIONS EXERCISE ====
This exercise combines multiple concepts: generics, references, and complex logic.

Your task:
Implement advanced function patterns

exercises.name: control_flow1
exercises.description:
==== CONTROL FLOW EXERCISE ====
Control flow in Move uses if/else expressions.
Unlike statements, expressions return values!

Your task:
Implement functions using if/else control flow.
